1.1: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better then wine.
1.2: Because of the sauour of thy good ointments thy name is as an ointment powred out: therefore the virgins love thee.
1.3: Draw me: we will runne after thee: the King hath brought me into his chabers: we will reioyce and be glad in thee: we will remember thy love more then wine: the righteous do love thee.
1.4: I am black, O daughters of Jerusalem, but comely, as the tentes of Kedar, and as the curtaines of Salomon.
1.5: Regard ye me not because I am black: for the sunne hath looked upon mee. The sonnes of my mother were angry against mee: they made me the keeper of ye vines: but I kept not mine own vine.
1.6: Shew me, O thou, whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou liest at noon: for why should I be as she that turneth aside to the flockes of thy companions?
1.7: If thou know not, O thou the fairest among women, get thee foorth by the steps of the flock, and feed thy kiddes by the tents of the shepheards.
1.8: I have compared thee, O my love, to the troupe of horses in the charets of Pharaoh.
1.9: Thy cheekes are comely with rowes of stones, and thy neck with chaines.
1.10: We will make thee borders of gold with studdes of silver.
1.11: Whiles the King was at his repast, my spikenard gave the smell thereof.
1.12: My welbeloued is as a bundle of myrrh unto me: he shall lie between my breasts.
1.13: My welbeloued is as a cluster of camphire unto me in the vines of Engedi.
1.14: My love, behold, thou art fair: behold, thou art fair: thine eyes are like the doves.
1.15: My welbeloued, behold, thou art fair and pleasant: also our bed is green:
1.16: The beames of our house are cedars, our rafters are of fire.

2.1: I am the rose of the field, and the lilie of the valleys.
2.2: Like a lilie amog the thornes, so is my love among the daughters.
2.3: Like the apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my welbeloued among the sonnes of men: under his shadow had I delite, and sat down: and his fruit was sweet unto my mouth.
2.4: Hee brought mee into the wine cellar, and love was his banner over me.
2.5: Stay me with flagons, and comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.
2.6: His left hand is under mine head, and his right hand doeth imbrace me.
2.7: I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and by the hindes of the field, that ye stirre not up, nor waken my love, until she please.
2.8: It is the voyce of my welbeloued: behold, hee cometh leaping by the mountaines, and skipping by the hilles.
2.9: My welbeloued is like a roe, or a yong hart: loe, he standeth behind our wall, looking forth of the windowes, shewing him self through the grates.
2.10: My welbeloued spake and said unto me, Arise, my love, my fair one, and come thy way.
2.11: For behold, winter is past: the rain is changed, and is gone away.
2.12: The flowers appear in the earth: the time of the singing of birdes is come, and the voyce of the turtle is heard in our land.
2.13: The figtree hath brought foorth her yong figges: and the vines with their small grapes have cast a sauour: arise my love, my fair one, and come away.
2.14: My dove, that art in the holes of ye rock, in the secret places of the staires, shew mee thy sight, let mee hear thy voyce: for thy voyce is sweet, and thy sight comely.
2.15: Take us the foxes, the little foxes, which destroy the vines: for our vines have small grapes.
2.16: My welbeloued is mine, and I am his: hee feedeth among the lilies,
2.17: Until the day break, and the shadowes flee away: return, my welbeloued, and be like a roe, or a yong hart upon the mountaines of Bether.

3.1: In my bed by night I sought him that my soul loved: I sought him, but I found him not.
3.2: I will rise therefore now, and goe about in the citie, by the streetes and by the open places, and wil seek him that my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.
3.3: The watchmen that went about the citie, found mee: to whom I said, Have you seen him, whom my soul loveth?
3.4: When I had past a litle from them, then I found him whom my soul loved: I took hold on him and left him not, till I had brought him unto my mothers house into the chamber of her that conceived me.
3.5: I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and by the hindes of the field, that ye stirre not up, nor waken my love until she please.
3.6: Who is she that cometh up out of the wildernes like pillars of smoke perfumed with myrrh and incense, and with all the spices of the marchant?
3.7: Behold his bed, which is Salomons: threescore strong men are round about it, of the valiant men of Israel.
3.8: They all handle the sword, and are expert in war, every one hath his sword upon his thigh for the fear by night.
3.9: King Salomon made himself a palace of the trees of Lebanon.
3.10: Hee made the pillars thereof of silver, and the pavement thereof of gold, the hangings thereof of purple, whose middes was paved with the love of the daughters of Jerusalem.
3.11: Come forth, ye daughters of Zion, and behold the King Salomon with the crown, wherewith his mother crowned him in ye day of his mariage, and in the day of the gladnes of his heart.

4.1: Behold, thou art fair, my love: behold, thou art fair: thine eyes are like the doves: among thy lockes thine hear is like the flock of goates, which look down from the mountain of Gilead.
4.2: Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep in good order, which go up from the washing: which every one bring out twinnes, and none is barren among them.
4.3: Thy lippes are like a threede of scarlet, and thy talk is comely: thy temples are within thy lockes as a piece of a pomegranate.
4.4: Thy neck is as the tower of David built for defence: a thousand shieldes hang therein, and all the targates of the strong men.
4.5: Thy two breastes are as two young roes that are twinnes, feeding among the lilies.
4.6: Until the day break, and the shadowes flie away, I wil go into the mountain of myrrh and to the mountain of incense.
4.7: Thou art all fair, my love, and there is no spot in thee.
4.8: Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, even with me from Lebanon, and look from the toppe of Amanah, from the toppe of Shenir and Hermon, from the dennes of the lyons, and from the mountaines of the leopards.
4.9: My sister, my spouse, thou hast wounded mine heart: thou hast wounded mine heart with one of thine eyes, and with a chain of thy neck.
4.10: My sister, my spouse, how fair is thy love? how much better is thy love then wine? and the sauour of thine oyntments then all spices?
4.11: Thy lippes, my spouse, droppe as honie combes: honie and milk are under thy tongue, and the sauoure of thy garments is as the sauoure of Lebanon.
4.12: My sister my spouse is as a garden inclosed, as a spring shut up, and a fountain sealed up.
4.13: Thy plantes are as an orchard of pomegranates with sweet fruites, as camphire, spikenard,
4.14: Even spikenard, and saffran, calamus, and cynamon with all the trees of incense, myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices.
4.15: O fountain of the gardens, O well of living waters, and the springs of Lebanon.
4.16: Arise, O North, and come O South, and blow on my garden that the spices thereof may flow out: let my welbeloued come to his garden, and eat his pleasant fruit.

5.1: I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I gathered my myrrh with my spice: I ate mine hony combe with mine hony, I drank my wine with my milk: eat, O friends, drink, and make you merie, O welbeloued.
5.2: I sleep, but mine heart waketh, it is the voyce of my welbeloued that knocketh, saying, Open unto mee, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for mine head is full of dew, and my lockes with the droppes of the night.
5.3: I have put off my coat, how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?
5.4: My welbeloued put in his hand by the hole of the door, and mine heart was affectioned toward him.
5.5: I rose up to open to my welbeloued, and mine hands did drop down myrrh, and my fingers pure myrrh upon the handels of the bar.
5.6: I opened to my welbeloued: but my welbeloued was gone, and past: mine heart was gone when hee did speak: I sought him, but I could not find him: I called him, but hee answered mee not.
5.7: The watchmen that went about the citie, found me: they smote me and wounded me: the watchmen of the walles took away my vail from me.
5.8: I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my welbeloued, that you tell him that I am sick of love.
5.9: O the fairest among women, what is thy welbeloued more then other welbeloued? what is thy welbeloued more then another lover, that thou doest so charge us?
5.10: My welbeloued is white and ruddie, the chiefest of ten thousand.
5.11: His head is as fine gold, his lockes curled, and black as a raven.
5.12: His eyes are like doves upon the rivers of waters, which are washt with milk, and remain by the full vessels.
5.13: His cheekes are as a bedde of spices, and as sweet flowres, and his lippes like lilies dropping down pure myrrh.
5.14: His hands as rings of gold set with the chrysolite, his belly like white yuorie covered with saphirs.
5.15: His legges are as pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold: his countenance as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars.
5.16: His mouth is as sweet thinges, and hee is wholy delectable: this is my welbeloued, and this is my lover, O daughters of Jerusalem.
5.17: O the fairest among women, whither is thy welbeloued gone? whither is thy welbeloued turned aside, that we may seek him with thee?

6.1: My welbeloued is gone down into his garden to the beds of spices, to feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies.
6.2: I am my welbeloueds, and my welbeloued is mine, who feedeth among the lilies.
6.3: Thou art beautiful, my love, as Tirzah, comely as Ierusale, terrible as an army with baners.
6.4: Turn away thine eyes from me: for they overcome mee: thine hear is like a flock of goates, which look down from Gilead.
6.5: Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep, which goe up from the washing, which every one bring out twinnes, and none is barren among them.
6.6: Thy temples are within thy lockes as a piece of a pomegranate.
6.7: There are threescore Queenes and fourescore concubines and of the damsels without nober.
6.8: But my dove is alone, and my undefiled, she is the onely daughter of her mother, and she is dear to her that bare her: the daughters have seen her and counted her blessed: even the Queenes and the concubines, and they have praised her.
6.9: Who is she that looketh foorth as the morning, fayre as the moon, pure as the sunne, terrible as an armie with banners!
6.10: I went down to the garden of nuttes, to see the fruites of the valley, to see if the vine budded, and if the pomegranates flourished.
6.11: I knew nothing, my soul set me as the charets of my noble people.
6.12: Return, return, O Shulamite, return: return that we may behold thee. What shall you see in the Shulamite, but as the company of an armie?

7.1: How beautiful are thy goings with shooes, O princes daughter! the ioynts of thy thighs are like jewels: the work of the hand of a cunning workeman.
7.2: Thy navel is as a round cuppe that wanteth not licour: thy belly is as an heap of wheat compassed about with lilies.
7.3: Thy two breastes are as two young roes that are twinnes.
7.4: Thy neck is like a towre of yuorie: thine eyes are like the fish pooles in Heshbon by the gate of Bath-rabbim: thy nose is as the towre of Lebanon, that looketh toward Damascus.
7.5: Thine head upon thee is as skarlet, and the bush of thine head like purple: the King is tyed in the rafters.
7.6: How fair art thou, and how pleasant art thou, O my love, in pleasures!
7.7: This thy stature is like a palm tree, and thy brestes like clusters.
7.8: I said, I will goe up into the palm tree, I will take hold of her boughes: thy breastes shall now be like the clusters of the vine: and the sauour of thy nose like apples,
7.9: And the roufe of thy mouth like good wine, which goeth straight to my welbeloued, and causeth the lippes of the ancient to speak.
7.10: I am my welbeloueds, and his desire is toward mee.
7.11: Come, my welbeloued, let us go foorth into the field: let us remain in the villages.
7.12: Let us get up early to the vines, let us see if the vine florish, whether it hath budded the small grape, or whether the pomegranates florish: there will I give thee my love.
7.13: The mandrakes have given a smell, and in our gates are all sweet things, new and old: my welbeloued, I have kept them for thee.

8.1: Oh that thou werest as my brother that sucked the brestes of my mother: I would find thee without, I would kiss thee, then they should not despise thee.
8.2: I will lead thee and bring thee into my mothers house: there thou shalt teach me: and I will cause thee to drink spiced wine, and new wine of the pomegranate.
8.3: His left hand shalbe under mine head, and his right hand shall embrace me.
8.4: I charge you, O daughters of Ierusale, that you stir not up, nor waken my love, until she please.
8.5: (Who is this that cometh up out of the wilderness, leaning upon her welbeloued?) I raysed thee up under an apple tree: there thy mother conceived thee: there she coceiued that bare thee.
8.6: Set mee as a seal on thine heart, and as a signet upon thine arm: for love is strong as death: ielousie is cruel as the grave: the coles thereof are fierie coles, and a vehement flame.
8.7: Much water can not quench love, neither can the floods drown it: If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, they would greatly contemn it.
8.8: Wee have a litle sister, and she hath no breastes: what shall we do for our sister when she shalbe spoken for?
8.9: If she be a wall, we will build upon her a silver palace: and if she be a door, we wil keep her in with bordes of cedar.
8.10: I am a wall, and my breasts are as towres: then was I in his eyes as one that findeth peace.
8.11: Salomon had a vine in Baal-hamon: hee gave the vineyard unto keepers: every one bringeth for ye fruit thereof a thousand pieces of silver.
8.12: But my vineyard which is mine, is before me: to thee, O Salomon appertaineth a thousand pieces of silver, and two hundreth to them that keep the fruit thereof.
8.13: O thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken unto thy voyce: cause me to hear it.
8.14: O my welbeloued, flee away, and be like unto the roe, or to the yong hart upon ye mountaines of spices.

22:1:1: This is spoken in the person of the Church, or of the faithful soul inflamed with the desire of Christ, whom she loveth.
Hebrew, a song of songs: so called because it is the chiefest of those 1005, which Solomon made, as is mentioned, I Kings 4:32.
22:1:2: They that are pure in heart and conversation.
The feeling of thy great benefits.
22:1:3: The faithful confess that they cannot come to Christ, except they be drawn.
Meaning, the secret joy that is not known to the world.
22:1:4: Kedar was Ishmael’s son, of whom came the Arabians that dwelt in tents.
Which within were all set with precious stones and Jewels.
The Church confesseth her spots and sin, but hath confidence in the favor of Christ.
22:1:5: The corruption of nature through sin and afflictions.
Mine own brethren, which should have most favored me.
Consider not the Church by the outward appearance.
22:1:6: Whom thou hast called to the dignity of pastors, and they set forth their own dreams instead of thy doctrine.
The spouse feeling her fault fleeth to her husband only for succor.
22:1:7: Christ speaketh to his Church, bidding them that are ignorant, to go to the pastors to learn.
22:1:8: For thy spiritual beauty and excellency there was no worldly treasure to be compared unto thee.
22:1:11: The Church rejoiceth that she is admitted to the company of Christ.
22:1:12: He shall be most dear unto me.
22:1:14: Christ accepteth his Church, and commendeth her beauty.
22:1:15: That is, the heart of the faithful, wherein Christ dwelleth by his Spirit.
22:2:2: Thus Christ preferreth his Church above all other things.
22:2:3: The spouse testifieth her great desire toward her husband, but her strength faileth her, and therefore she desireth to be comforted, and felt it.
22:2:7: Christ chargeth them which have to do in the Church as it were by a solemn oath, that they trouble not the quietness thereof.
22:2:8: This is spoken of Christ, who took upon his our nature to come to help his Church.
22:2:9: Forasmuch as his divinity was hid under the cloak of our flesh.
So that we cannot have full knowledge of him in this life.
22:2:11: That is, sin and error is driven back by the coming of Christ, which is here described by the spring time, when all things flourish.
22:2:14: Thou that art ashamed of thy sins, come and show thyself unto me.
22:2:15: Suppress the heretics while they are young, that is, when they begin to show their malice, and destroy the vine of the Lord.
22:2:17: The Church desireth Christ to be most ready to help her in all dangers.
22:3:1: The Church by night, that is, in troubles, seeketh to Christ, but is not incontinently heard.
22:3:2: Showing that although we be not heard at the first, yet we must still continue in prayer, till we feel comfort.
22:3:3: Which declareth that we must seek unto all of whom we hope to have any succor.
22:3:6: This is referred to the Church of Israel, which was led by the wilderness forty years.
22:3:7: By the bed is meant the Temple which Solomon made.
22:3:8: He alludeth to the watch which kept the Temple.
22:3:11: All ye that are of the number of the faithful.
Christ become man was crowned by the love of God with the glorious crown of his divinity.
22:4:1: He hath respect to the multitude of the faithful, which are many in number.
Because Christ delighteth in his Church, he commendeth all that is in her.
22:4:5: Wherein are knowledge and zeal two precious jewels.
22:4:8: Christ promiseth his Church to call his faithful from all the corners of the world.
22:4:9: In that he made his Church beautiful and rich, he loved his gifts in her.
Christ calleth his Church sister, in respect that he had taken the flesh of man.
22:4:11: Because of thy confession and thanksgiving.
22:4:15: The Church confesseth that all her glory and beauty cometh of Christ, who is the true fountain of all grace.
22:4:16: She desireth Christ to comfort her and to pour the graces of his Spirit upon her, which Spirit is meant by the North and South wind.
22:5:1: The garden signifieth the kingdom of Christ, where he prepareth the banquet for his elect.
22:5:2: The spouse saith that she is troubled with the cares of worldly things, which is meant by sleeping.
Declaring the long patience of the Lord toward sinners.
22:5:3: The spouse confesseth her nakedness, and that of herself she hath nothing, or seeing that she is once made clean, she promiseth not to defile herself again.
22:5:4: Hebrew, my bowels were moved towards him.
22:5:5: The spouse which should be anointed of Christ, shall not find him if she think to anoint him with her good works.
22:5:7: These are the false teachers, which wound the conscience with their traditions.
22:5:8: She asketh of them which are godly (forasmuch as the law and salvation should come out of Zion and Jerusalem) that they would direct her to Christ.
22:5:11: She describeth Christ to be of perfect beauty and comeliness.
22:5:17: Hearing of the excellency of Christ, the faithful desire to know how to find him.
22:6:1: That is, is conversant here in earth among men.
22:6:3: Which was a fair and strong city, 1 Kings 14:17.
22:6:4: This declareth the exceeding love of Christ toward his Church.
22:6:7: Meaning, that the gifts are infinite which Christ giveth to his Church: or that his faithful are many in number
22:6:9: He showeth that the beginning of the Church was small, but that it grew up to a great multitude.
22:6:10: He went down into the Synagogue to see what fruits came of the Law, and the Prophets.
22:6:11: Or, set me on the chariots of my willing people.
22:6:12: O ye people of Jerusalem: for Jerusalem was called Salem which signifieth peace.
22:7:1: He describeth the comely beauty of the Church in every part, which is to be understood spiritually.
22:7:5: He delighteth to come near thee, and to be in thy company.
22:7:12: If the people that are called to Christ, bring forth any fruit.
22:8:1: The Church called of the Gentiles, speaketh thus to the Church of Jerusalem.
22:8:6: The spouse desireth Christ to be joined in perpetual love with him.
22:8:8: The Jewish Church speaketh this of the Church of the Gentiles.
22:8:9: If she be sure and fast, she is meet for the husband to dwell in.
22:8:10: The Church promiseth fidelity and constancy.
22:8:11: This is the vineyard of the Lord hired out, Matt. 21:33.
22:8:13: Christ dwelleth in his Church, whose voice the faithful hear.
22:8:14: The Church desireth Christ that if he depart from them, yet that he would haste to help them in their troubles.
